'''''Chlorella vulgaris''''' is a species of green [[microalga]] in the division [[Chlorophyta]].<ref name="safi2014">{{cite journal|author=Safi, C., Zebib, B., Merah, O., Pontalier, P. Y., & Vaca-Garcia, C. |title= Morphology, composition, production, processing and applications of ''Chlorella vulgaris'': A review|journal= Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews|volume= 35|pages= 265–278| doi= 10.1016/j.rser.2014.04.007|year= 2014|bibcode= 2014RSERv..35..265S|url= https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-02064882/file/Safi_23269.pdf}}</ref> This unicellular alga was discovered in 1890 by [[Martinus Beijerinck|Martinus Willem Beijerinck]]<ref>{{cite journal|author=Beijerinck, M. W. |year=1890|title= Culturversuche mit Zoochlorellen, Lichenengonidien und anderen niederen Algen|journal= Bot. Zeitung|volume= 48|pages= 781–785}}</ref> as the first microalga with a well-defined nucleus.<ref name=safi2014/> It is the type species of the genus ''[[Chlorella]]''.<ref name=Kreinitz2015>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/j.tplants.2014.11.005 |title=''Chlorella'': 125 years of the green survivalist |year=2015 |last1=Krienitz |first1=Lothar |last2=Huss |first2=Volker A.R. |last3=Bock |first3=Christina |journal=Trends in Plant Science |volume=20 |issue=2 |pages=67–69 |pmid=25500553 |bibcode=2015TPS....20...67K }}</ref> It is found in [[freshwater]] and terrestrial habitats, and has a [[cosmopolitan distribution]].<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.3389/fmicb.2020.585836|doi-access=free |title=Adaptation to Aquatic and Terrestrial Environments in ''Chlorella vulgaris'' (Chlorophyta) |date=2020 |last1=Aigner |first1=Siegfried |last2=Glaser |first2=Karin |last3=Arc |first3=Erwann |last4=Holzinger |first4=Andreas |last5=Schletter |first5=Michael |last6=Karsten |first6=Ulf |last7=Kranner |first7=Ilse |journal=Frontiers in Microbiology |volume=11 |pmid=33178169 |pmc=7593248 }}</ref>

''Chlorella vulgaris'' has a number of potential applications in science, such as [[biofuel]], [[livestock feed]], and [[wastewater treatment]].<ref name=safi2014/> Beginning in the 1990s, German scientists noticed the high [[protein]] content of ''C. vulgaris'' and began to consider it as a new food source. Japan is currently the largest consumer of ''Chlorella'',<ref name="safi2014" /><ref name="kitada2009">{{cite journal|author=Kitada, K., Machmudah, S., Sasaki, M., Goto, M., Nakashima, Y., Kumamoto, S., & Hasegawa, T. |title=Supercritical CO<sub>2</sub> extraction of pigment components with pharmaceutical importance from ''Chlorella vulgaris''|doi=10.1002/jctb.2096|journal=Journal of Chemical Technology and Biotechnology|volume=84|issue=5|pages=657–661|year=2009|bibcode=2009JCTB...84..657K }}</ref> both for nutritional and therapeutic purposes,<ref name="Freitas-2017">{{Cite journal|last=Freitas|first=Hércules Rezende|date=2017-08-25|title=Chlorella vulgaris as a Source of Essential Fatty Acids and Micronutrients: A Brief Commentary|url=https://benthamopen.com/ABSTRACT/TOPSJ-10-92|journal=The Open Plant Science Journal|volume=10|issue=1|pages=92–99 |doi= 10.2174/1874294701710010092 |doi-broken-date=11 July 2025 |doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and it is used as a [[dietary supplement]] or [[protein]]-rich [[food additive]] in several countries worldwide.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1111/1750-3841.17529|pmc=11673457 |title=''Chlorella vulgaris'' as a food substitute: Applications and benefits in the food industry |date=2024 |last1=Wang |first1=Chiao-An |last2=Onyeaka |first2=Helen |last3=Miri |first3=Taghi |last4=Soltani |first4=Fakhteh |journal=Journal of Food Science |volume=89 |issue=12 |pages=8231–8247 |pmid=39556490 }}</ref>

==Description==
''C. vulgaris'' is a green [[Eukaryote|eukaryotic]] microalga. The cells are 4–10 μm in diameter, and are spherical. The [[chloroplast]] (chromatophore) is pea-green in color and cup-shaped, with a single [[pyrenoid]].<ref name=Shihira>{{cite book|title= Chlorella. Physiology and taxonomy of forty-one isolates|date=1965|last1= Shihira|first1=I.|last2=Krauss|first2=R.W.|location=Maryland|publisher= University of Maryland, College Park|pages=1–97}}</ref>

== Symbiosis ==
''Chlorella vulgaris'' occurs as a [[Symbiosis|symbiont]] in tissues of the freshwater [[flatworm]]s ''[[Dalyellia viridis]] and [[Typhloplana viridata]]''.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Young|first=J. O.|title=Keys to the freshwater microturbellarians of Britain and Ireland|publisher=Freshwater Biological Association|year=2001|location=Ambleside|page=92}}</ref>

==Production==
The world annual production of the various species of ''[[Chlorella]]'' was 2000 tonnes (dry weight) in 2009, with the main producers being Germany, Japan and Taiwan.<ref name="safi2014" /> ''C. vulgaris'' is a candidate for commercial production due to its high resistance against adverse conditions and invading organisms. In addition, the production of the various organic macromolecules of interest (proteins, lipids, starch) differ depending on the technique used to create biomass and can be therefore targeted.<ref name="safi2014" /> Under more hostile conditions, the biomass decreases, but lipids and starch contents increase.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Přibyl, P., Cepak, V., & Zachleder, V. |title= Production of lipids in 10 strains of ''Chlorella'' and ''Parachlorella'', and enhanced lipid productivity in ''Chlorella vulgaris''|journal= Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology|volume= 94|issue= 2|pages= 549–61| doi=10.1007/s00253-012-3915-5|pmid=22361856|year= 2012|s2cid= 16442599}}</ref> Under nutrient and light-replete conditions, protein content increases along with the biomass.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Yuvraj |author2=Ambarish Sharan Vidyarthi |author3=Jeeoot Singh |year=2016 |title=Enhancement of Chlorella vulgaris cell density: Shake flask and bench-top photobioreactor studies to identify and control limiting factors |journal=Korean Journal of Chemical Engineering |volume=33 |issue=8 |pages=2396–2405 |doi=10.1007/s11814-016-0087-5 |s2cid=99110136 }}</ref> Different growth techniques have been developed. Different modes of growth (autotrophic, heterotrophic, and mixotrophic) has been investigated for ''Chlorella vulgaris''; autotrophic growth is favoured as it does not require provision of costly organic carbon and relies on inorganic carbon sources ({{CO2}}, carbonates) and light for photosynthesis.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Yuvraj |author2=Padmini Padmanabhan |year=2017 |title=Technical insight on the requirements for {{CO2}}-saturated growth of microalgae in photobioreactors |journal=3 Biotech |volume=07 |issue=2 |page=119 |doi=10.1007/s13205-017-0778-6 |pmid=28567633 |pmc=5451369 }}</ref>

''Chlorella sp.'' cultivated in digested and membrane-pretreated swine manure is capable of improving the growth medium performance of microalgae cultivations in terms of final [[biomass productivity]], showing that algal growth depends on the turbidity of liquid digestate streams rather than on their nutrient availability.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Claudio|last1=Ledda|first2=Antonio|last2=Ida|first3=Donatella|last3=Allemand|first4=Paola|last4=Mariani|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/281314164|title=Production of wild Chlorella sp. cultivated in digested and membrane-pretreated swine manure derived from a full-scale operation plant|format=PDF|page=Abstract, 70|journal=Algal Research|volume=12|date=November 1, 2015|doi=10.1016/j.algal.2015.08.010|bibcode=2015AlgRe..12...68L |issn=	2211-9264|oclc=5878756379|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210808172700/https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Paola-Mariani-3/publication/281314164_Production_of_wild_Chlorella_sp_cultivated_in_digested_and_membrane-pretreated_swine_manure_derived_from_a_full-scale_operation_plant/links/5a69de800f7e9b01f3ee6628/Production-of-wild-Chlorella-sp-cultivated-in-digested-and-membrane-pretreated-swine-manure-derived-from-a-full-scale-operation-plant.pdf|archive-date=August 8, 2021|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Uses==

===Bioremediation===
''Chlorella vulgaris'' has been the microalgae of choice for several [[bioremediation]] processes. Owing to its ability to remove a variety of pollutants such as inorganic nutrients (nitrate, nitrite, phosphate and ammonium), fertilizers, detergents, heavy metals, pesticides, pharmaceuticals and other emerging pollutants from wastewater and effluents, carbon dioxide and other gaseous pollutants from flue gases, besides having high growth rates and simple cultivation requirements, ''Chlorella vulgaris'' has emerged as a potential microorganism in bioremediation studies for mitigation of environmental pollution.<ref name="yuvraj 305 318">{{cite book | vauthors = Yuvraj | chapter = Microalgal Bioremediation: A Clean and Sustainable Approach for Controlling Environmental Pollution|date=2022 |volume=1|pages=305–318| title = Innovations in Environmental Biotechnology|place=Singapore|publisher=Springer Singapore|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-981-16-4445-0_13|isbn=978-981-16-4445-0 }}</ref>

===Bioenergy===
''C. vulgaris'' is seen as a promising source of [[bioenergy]]. It may be a good alternative to [[biofuel]] crops, like soybean, corn or rapeseed, as it is more productive and does not compete with food production.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Singh, A., Nigam, P. S., & Murphy, J. D. |title= Renewable fuels from algae: An answer to debatable land based fuels|journal= Bioresource Technology|volume= 102|issue= 1|pages= 10–16|doi= 10.1016/j.biortech.2010.06.032|pmid= 20615690|year= 2011|bibcode= 2011BiTec.102...10S}}</ref> It can produce large amount of [[lipid]]s, up to 20 times more than crops<ref>{{cite journal|author=Demirbas, M. F. |title= Biofuels from algae for sustainable development|journal= Applied Energy|volume= 88|issue= 10|pages= 3473–3480|doi= 10.1016/j.apenergy.2011.01.059|year= 2011|bibcode= 2011ApEn...88.3473D}}</ref> that have a suitable profile for [[biodiesel]] production.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Wang, K. G., Brown, R. C., Homsy, S., Martinez, L., & Sidhu, S. S.|title= Fast pyrolysis of microalgae remnants in a fluidized bed reactor for bio-oil and biochar production|journal= Bioresource Technology|volume= 127|pages= 494–499|doi= 10.1016/j.biortech.2012.08.016|pmid= 23069615|year= 2013|bibcode= 2013BiTec.127..494W}}</ref> This microalgae also contains high amounts of [[starch]], good for the production of [[Ethanol|bioethanol]].<ref name="safi2014" /> However, microalgal biofuels are far from competitive with fossil fuels, given their high production costs and controversial sustainability.<ref name="safi2014" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://newatlas.com/environment/algae-fueled-bioreactor-carbon-sequestration/|title=Algae-fueled bioreactor soaks up {{CO2}} 400x more effectively than trees|last=Lavars|first=Nick|date=2019-09-19|website=New Atlas|language=en|access-date=2019-10-04}}</ref>
